Imagine all the things that are priced into BTC and crypto as a whole right now:

1) A hawkish Fed, hot inflation, rising yields, a stronger dollar and shrinking stablecoin supply.

2) Post-midterm regulatory uncertainty now that Democrats control Congress, and with it the risk of a new crackdown.

3) Cybersecurity and quantum risk higher than ever, with the biggest hack in history at Binance and exploits getting more frequent across the board.

4) The bloated AI trade starting to unwind, threatening to drag everything around it down.

I'm probably even missing something. It’s hard to imagine it getting much worse, but at the same time things are rarely as bad as they seem.

Honestly, I'm rather even impressed by how much strength crypto is showing through all of this. We've seen far worse sell offs for far lighter reasons.

The window of max opportunity is right now.

Take it or leave it.

tweets.text:
I think if we take seriously the idea that we're going into a cybersecurity apocalypse in 2027, then the volume of coin thefts is going to be higher than before, and so it's prudent to be more cautious than we were planning to be 6 months ago

To me privacy pools type tech is a good keyhole solution: it serves the goal of making thieves' lives significantly harder (though it may require harsher measures: 24h deposit delay, and charge some small fee on rejection) without doing the really harmful thing: backdoors.

No backdoors is the line that is defensible as an absolute.

Long-term though, we really need to upgrade everyone to much safer storage formats for coins.

GDP only grows three ways... more people, more debt or more productivity. 

More people is gone. Demographics were set in stone 30 years ago and nobody can change them. The workforce is shrinking and ageing, so the growth that used to come from simply adding workers has been fading for two decades.

For the last 15 years the gap left by people has been filled with borrowing, more and more of it, until we're now borrowing to pay the interest on the borrowing. That's the debasement everyone feels but cant name. And that lever is spent too.

Which leaves the third one. Productivity. But here's the problem... productivity has always meant people producing more, and we are running out of people. The only way to get a step change in output with fewer workers is machines.

AI and robotics are not a nice to have. They are the one lever still available, and they are the only thing that can get us out of this mess and outgrow the debt rather than inflate it away.

So yes, people are worried about the robots taking their jobs. The alternative is a system with no way out.

What does change is who the value flows to. It goes to whoever owns the networks...

So if the robots are coming for our jobs, then we had bloody well better own the robots.

NVIDIA doesn’t own a fab. Its edge is a supply chain that took one product from $1 billion to $250 billion. Even so, it will probably lose share.

“What really keeps them in the game is supply chain. It’s feeling a lot like Apple in 2020. People are perceiving them as having a lot of competition.”

“A lab is not really capable of ramping a product from a billion to 250 billion dollars. NVIDIA is a one-of-one company that’s done that, and there’s a lot of chops that go into that.”

“I do think that share gain against NVIDIA is extremely possible, and probably probable now.”

“Using AI to make your chip better, that’s the future for sure. NVIDIA wants to fight back against it as hard as they can, but it remains to be seen.”
